original_value: Over the last two decades there has been a proliferation of methods for simulating crowds of humans. As the number of different methods and their complexity increases, it becomes increasingly unrealistic to expect researchers and users to keep up with all the possible options and trade-offs. We therefore see the need for tools that can facilitate both domain experts and non-expert users of crowd simulation in making high-level decisions about the best simulation methods to use in different scenarios. In this paper, we leverage trajectory data from human crowds and machine learning techniques to learn a manifold which captures representative local navigation scenarios that humans encounter in real life. We show the applicability of this manifold in crowd research, including analyzing trends in simulation accuracy, and creating automated systems to assist in choosing an appropriate simulation method for a given scenario.

result.paraphrase: Over the past twenty years, methods for simulating human crowds have proliferated. As the variety and complexity of these approaches grows, it becomes less realistic to expect researchers and users to track all possible options and trade-offs. For this reason, we need tools that help both crowd-simulation experts and non-expert users make high-level choices about which methods are best suited to different scenarios. In this paper, we use trajectory data from human crowds together with machine learning to learn a manifold that captures representative local navigation scenarios people encounter in real life. We demonstrate how this manifold can be applied in crowd research, including examining trends in simulation accuracy and building automated systems to help select an appropriate simulation method for a given scenario.
